Introduction

Football has been a focal point of sports-related concussions (SRC) analysis and intervention.

                                                                                     T
Given the increased awareness of the long-term consequences of multiple concussions, SRCs

                                                                             IP
have gained increased societal interest over the past decade. In 1994 the National Football

League (NFL) established the Committee on Traumatic Brain Injury, which has focused on
                                                                        R
                                                             SC
reducing the incidence of SRCs [1]. More recently, the NFL Head, Neck and Spine Committee

was formed to address neurological issues relevant to the health and safety of active NFL

                                                        U
players. Similar to the NFL, the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) took steps to


                                            AN
address the issue of SRC, and in 2008 the organization instituted a “targeting” rule to decrease

the rate of SRC in football [2]. The 2008 NCAA “targeting” rule defined a foul as initiating

                                     M
contact with the crown of a helmet (Rule 9-1-3) or targeting a defenseless player in the head and

neck area (Rule 9-1-4) punishable by personal foul penalty. In 2013 the NCAA expanded Rule
                             D
9-1-4, targeting a defenseless player in the head and neck area, with violation of the rule
                   TE
resulting in an automatic ejection from the game [3].


         EP
Interestingly lower extremity injury rates in NCAA football players were observed to increase

   C
following institution of the “targeting” rule over 6 seasons [2]. The increased incidence of injury

AC
was most pronounced in ankle and knee injuries, particularly those that were secondary to player

contact [2]. However, the rates of noncontact/overuse injuries of the lower extremity did not

change [2]. The authors speculate that despite the aim of the targeting rule change to decrease

the incidence and severity of head trauma, it may have produced the unintended consequence of

increased lower extremity injuries [2].
 In response to the NCAA targeting rule and increasing number of diagnosed concussions in NFL

players, the NFL instituted playing rule article 8 prior to the 2018 season [4]. Playing rule article

8 aimed to help decrease SRC by broadening the helmet-hit rule, which now made it a foul when

                                                                                       T
a player lowers his head to make contact with his helmet against an opponent [4]. The rule states

                                                                               IP
that players found to be in violation of playing rule article 8 are to be penalized 15 yards and

subject to possible disqualification from the game, pending replay review.
                                                                          R
                                                              SC
The aim of this study was to quantify the impact of playing rule article 8 on lower extremity

                                                        U
injury rates among NFL players. Specifically, the objectives of this study were to determine if


                                               AN
playing rule article 8 unintentionally led to a significant increase in (1) the rate of lower

extremity injuries sustained by NFL players during regular season games, (2) the average games

                                        M
missed secondary to lower extremity injuries, and (3) the number of players placed on the injury

reserve for lower extremity injuries.
                              D
                    TE
When injury prevention interventions are instituted, such as rule changes, follow-up efficacy


         EP
studies are recommended [5]. With growing awareness of player safety and the dangers

associated with SRC, it is integral to quantify risk reduction in an objective manner. We
   C
hypothesized that rates of lower extremity injuries, average number of games missed, and

AC
percentage of players placed on IR would be significantly higher after the enactment of playing

rule article 8 as compared to prior seasons.



Methods

Data collection
 This study was a retrospective review of all NFL players who were placed on the injury report

for a lower extremity injury from the 2016-2017 through 2019-2020 NFL regular seasons. The

data was compiled using publicly available injury reports (Appendix). The sources used publish

weekly injury reports detailing the name of the players injured, their corresponding teams, and a

                                                                                       T
brief description of each injury. At least two different sources were used to cross-reference

                                                                               IP
injury information. To verify each player’s date of injury, we confirmed each player’s reported


                                                                         R
injury date corresponded to an absence of statistics from the respective games for which they


                                                              SC
were ruled out. These methods are in accordance with previously published protocols [6-10].



                                                        U
Team records available on individual team websites were used to collect demographic


                                             AN
information. Our dataset included each player’s name, position, team, pathology, age at injury,

date of injury, season, number of weeks missed due to injury, and date of return to play.

                                      M
With article 8 taking effect starting with the 2018-2019 season, players were assigned to a pre- or

post-rule cohort based on date of injury for purposes of injury rate comparison.
                              D
Definitions
                    TE
         EP
Reportable injuries were based on the criteria that the injury necessitated a team physician

referral or emergent care and resulted in missed athletic activity. Pre-season games were
   C
excluded from investigation to account for the potentially different level of competition during

AC
this time period, as well as for the inability to track players lost to follow-up due to being cut

from the team prior to the regular season. Additionally, post-season play was excluded so that

all teams had equal representation throughout the study period to eliminate potential confounding
 of injury rates due to team-specific playing style. An athlete-exposure (AE) was defined as one

athlete’s participation in one game in which they were exposed to potential injury.



Data and Statistical Analysis

                                                                                      T
Data analysis was conducted using SPSS 25 (SPSS Inc, Chicago, Illinois). Injury rates were

                                                                            IP
calculated per 1000 AEs using the following calculation: (Total number of lower extremity


                                                                      R
injuries (or SRC) x 1000/ Total number of AEs). Incidence rate ratio (RR) with 95% confidence


                                                                 SC
intervals (CI) compared injury rates between the two cohorts. Average number of games missed

and number of players placed on IR per year were also calculated. Continuous variables were

                                                        U
statistically compared using two-tailed t-test, while categorical variables were compared using


                                             AN
Chi-square test. Statistical significance was set at P ≤ 0.05.

Discussion
 As rule changes are implemented, quantifying rule efficacy in promoting player safety should be

vigorously evaluated. The purpose of this study was to determine if playing rule article 8

unintentionally led to a significant increase in (1) the rate of lower extremity injuries sustained

by NFL players during regular season games, (2) the average games missed secondary to lower

                                                                                      T
extremity injuries, and (3) the number of players placed on the injury reserve for lower extremity

                                                                              IP
injuries. We hypothesized that rates of lower extremity injuries, average number of games


                                                                         R
missed, and percentage of players placed on IR would be significantly higher after the enactment


                                                              SC
of playing rule article 8 as compared to prior. Our findings suggest that over the past two

seasons, the rate of lower extremity injuries and players placed on the IR for a lower extremity

                                                        U
injury has not significantly increased, however the average games missed due to lower extremity


                                             AN
injuries has significantly increased. Further the rate of SRC and average games missed due to

SRC has significantly decreased, and players placed on the IR due to SRC has not significantly

changed.                              M
                              D
NFL players were first to voice concerns regarding the targeting rule; they speculated that the
                    TE
rule change may lead to an unintentional increase in the rate of lower extremity injuries as


           EP
players, out of self-preservation and in an attempt to avoid head-on collisions, would opt to dive

at the ball carriers’ legs in order to make a tackle [11, 12]. Following this public criticism of the
   C
rule, in 2016 Westermann et al. investigated this claim and examined the rate of lower extremity

AC
injuries in NCAA football players following implementation of the targeting rule over six

seasons. The findings of Westermann et al. suggested that lower extremity injury rates increased

among NCAA football players after implementation of the targeting rule. Specifically, they

noted that knee and ankle injuries resulting from player contact increased significantly [3]. The
 findings of Westermann et al. supported NFL players speculations that the targeting rule may

increase the rate of lower extremity injuries. However, their study was not without limitation, to

which they acknowledge and highlight potential confounders. The most significant confounder

being the unintended effects of other policy changes made by the NCAA during the study period.

                                                                                    T
For example in 2012 the NCAA moved the kickoff up to the 35-yd line (previously at the 30-yd

                                                                             IP
line) in an attempt to decrease the rate of contact-related injuries. Although one can assume that


                                                                       R
this rule change would likely lead to more touchbacks, which in theory would reduce the risk of


                                                            SC
all contact related injuries. However, given these potential confounders further investigation in a

cohort of NFL players is warranted.

                                                       U
                                            AN
As mentioned previously we did not find a significant difference in the rate of lower extremity

injuries or players placed on the IR for a lower extremity injury over the past two NFL seasons

                                      M
under playing rule article 8. Our findings did note that the average games missed due to lower

extremity injuries has significantly increased. This suggests that the severity of lower extremity
                             D
injuries under playing rule article 8 has increased. However, this finding could also be
                   TE
secondary to a handful of players sustaining a season ending injury early in the season, and thus


         EP
missing more games, which we did not control for in this study. The number of players placed

on the IR for a lower extremity injury was higher under playing rule article 8 than the two
   C
previous seasons. However, the risk ratio of being placed on the IR for a lower extremity injury

AC
between our two cohorts was not significantly different. Despite this fact similar studies have

demonstrated NFL rule changes to have an appreciable effect on the rate of lower extremity

injuries in NFL athletes. Specifically, Baker et al. demonstrated that the NFL’s chop block rule

decreased the rate of lower extremity injuries in NFL defensive players [13]. Of note the chop
 block rule was instituted in 2015, thus it was not a confounding factor in this study. The findings

of Baker et al. demonstrate that NFL rule changes can affect injury patterns in players.



The effect of the targeting rule on lower extremity injuries in NFL players can be explained by

                                                                                     T
risk compensation theory. Risk compensation theory, first described by Hagel et al, suggests that

                                                                              IP
people adjust their behavior according to the perceived severity of risk and may be less cautious


                                                                        R
with respect to less risky behavior [14]. As it relates to the current study, head-to-head contact


                                                             SC
and SRC during a play are the perceived risks, thus players may be adjusting their behavior,

likely tackling form or body position upon contact, in order to avoid head-to-head contact.

                                                       U
Following implementation of the targeting rule one can speculate that the perceived severity of


                                            AN
risk of a head-to-head collision among football players is increased. The perceived increased

risk prompts players to adjust their tackling form in order to avoid head-to-head collisions.

                                      M
Football players altering their tackling form, specifically tackling low in order to avoid head-to-

head collisions, may increase the rate of lower extremity injuries in football players. This theory
                              D
regarding the targeting rule increasing rates of lower extremity injuries in NCAA football players
                   TE
is supported by the findings of Westermann et al. In the current study, the observed rate of lower


         EP
extremity injuries following the enactment of the targeting rule did not significantly increase.

We speculate that this finding can be explained by a possible difference in perceived severity of
   C
risk of a head-to-head collision between collegiate and NFL football players. Our findings

AC
suggest that NFL players either do not perceive the risk of a head-to-head collision to be as

severe as collegiate players and thus have not adjusted their tackling style to favor low tackles, or

NFL players are, on average, more talented athletes and tackle with safer tackling form.

However, neither of these speculations offer a good explanation of why players missed
 significantly more games due to LEI following institution of the targeting rule; this finding,

though, may be related to timing of injury rather than severity, as mentioned previously.



This study provides important insight regarding patterns and injury rates in professional football

                                                                                     T
players and can serve as a benchmark for discussion about injury prevention. To our knowledge,

                                                                             IP
no other study has focused on rule article 8 and its effect on lower extremity injury rates in NFL


                                                                        R
players. Over the past century football has implemented rule changes, like the targeting and chop


                                                             SC
block rule, in order to improve player safety. Most notably in 1939 the National Collegiate

Athletic Association (NCAA) made football helmets mandatory [2]. However, the most

                                                       U
dramatic effect on player safety wasn’t noted until the late 1970s when “spearing” was forbidden


                                             AN
in order to improve the head position of defensive players when tackling. The “spearing” rule

led to a significant decrease in the incidence of spinal cord injuries, demonstrating the powerful

                                      M
effect of rule changes on injuries in football [16].


                              D
Our study demonstrated that under playing rule article 8 the overall rate of SRC has decreased,
                    TE
while the average number of games missed and number of players placed on IR for a SRC did


         EP
not significantly change. Similar to lower extremity injuries the average number of games missed

and number of players placed on the IR reflects severity of injury. Thus, our study suggests that
   C
playing rule article 8 has significantly lowered concussion rate but not severity.

AC
Since 2012 the NFL has publicly released injury data analyzed by IQVIA, an independent third-

party company retained by the NFL [12]. The data published includes the incidence of reported

concussions during the preseason and regular season. In comparing our data to the regular
 seasons data published by the NFL we noted that the NFL reported a higher rate of SRC for both

the 2016-2017 to 2017-2018 and 2018-2019 to 2019-2020 cohorts (6.6 versus 5.5, and 5.1 versus

3.3 per 1,000 AEs; NFL compared to our data respectively). The data published by the NFL

has been instituted, albeit less dramatically.                                        T
                                                                              IP
                                                                         R
The discrepancy between our data and the data published by the NFL calls into question the


                                                              SC
validity of gathering publicly available data from injury reports to draw conclusions about

injuries in professional athletes. However, this observation may in part be due to how the

                                                        U
publishing of NFL injury reports work. It is important to note that NFL teams typically publish


                                             AN
their first weekly injury report on Tuesday of each week, which is two days after a Sunday game

but five days after a Thursday game. Thus, minor injuries sustained during NFL games that

                                      M
resolve during the 2-5-day period before the injury report is published would not be captured by

the injury report, but may be captured by the NFL’s own dataset. If twenty percent of the
                              D
injuries reported by IQVIA resolved in the 2-5-day period before publication of team injury
                    TE
reports, it would fully explain the lower number of SRC published on injury reports.


         EP
This study, as well as other similar publications utilizing the well-established multistep protocol
   C
to identify injuries in professional athletes through review of public records, is associated with

AC
several well-recognized limitations. Details regarding injury diagnosis and management,

including injury severity, exact pathology, imaging reports, and exact medical clearance were not

available for all players. Because injured players were identified using public records, the

possibility of reporting errors, and omissions exist. Study duration is a significant limitation as
 the study only spans four NFL seasons. Finally, there remains the possibility of selection bias in

the injured group in which only “newsworthy” players injured were reported on. We attempted

to control for this selection bias by only including regular season games, in order to account for

the inability to track players lost to follow-up due to being cut from the team prior to the regular

                                                                                        T
season. Further an attempt to minimize this bias was made by corroborating reported injuries

                                                                              IP
with two additional resources, but the data is limited by what is publicly available.


                                                                        R
Conclusion
                                                             SC
The rate of lower extremity and players placed on the IR over the past two NFL seasons

                                                       U
following the enactment of playing rule article 8 has not significantly increased. The average


                                            AN
games missed due to lower extremity injuries has significantly increased under playing rule

article 8, suggesting increased severity of injury. Further the rate of SRC and average games

98	
99	                                                    Physiological and psychological demands during training and competition generate fatigue and
100	
101	                                                    reduce an athlete´s sport-specific performance capacity. The magnitude of this decrement
102	
103	                                                    depends on several characteristics of the exercise stimulus (e.g. type, duration, intensity) as
104	
105	                                                    well as on individual characteristics (e. g. fitness, profile, fatigue resistance). As such, the time
106	
107	                                                    required to fully recover is proportional to the level of fatigue and the consequences of exercise-
108	
109	                                                    induced fatigue are manifold. Whatever the purpose of the ensuing exercise session (i.e.
110	
111	                                                    training or competition), it is crucial to understand the importance of optimizing the period
112	
113	                                                    between exercise bouts, in order to speed up the regenerative processes and facilitate recovery
114	
115	
116	
117	
118	Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 06/23/19
119	                                                    or set the next stimulus at the optimal time point. This implies having a fairly precise
120	
121	                                                    understanding of the fatigue mechanisms that contribute to the performance decrement. Failing
122	
123	                                                    to respect an athlete´s recovery needs may lead to an excessive accumulation of fatigue, and
124	
125	                                                    potentially “non-functional overreaching” or to maladaptive training. Although research in this
126	
127	                                                    area recently increased, considerations regarding the specific time frames for different
128	
129	                                                    physiological mechanisms in relation to exercise-induced fatigue are still missing.
130	
131	                                                    Furthermore, recommendations on the timing and dosing of recovery based on these time
132	
133	                                                    frames are limited. Therefore, the aim of this article is to describe time courses of recovery in
134	
135	                                                    relation to the exercise type and on different physiological levels. This summary shall support
136	
137	                                                    coaches, athletes and scientists in their decision-making process by considering the relationship
138	
139	                                                    of exercise type, physiology and recovery.
140	                                                     “The Temporal Relationship Between Exercise, Recovery Processes and Changes in Performance” by Skorski S et al.
141	                                                    International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
142	                                                    © 2019 Human Kinetics, Inc.
143	
144	
145	                                                    Introduction
146	
147	                                                             Each physical training session provides athletes with physiological stress, leading to
148	
149	                                                    disturbances in homeostasis of a number of physiological processes and biochemical pathways.
150	
151	                                                    In response to this stress, the body triggers post-exercise adaptive reactions that counteract
152	
153	                                                    these physiological and biochemical changes, emphasizing the necessity for an adequate
154	
155	                                                    recovery period after the training bout. For the purposes of this commentary fatigue is defined
156	
157	                                                    as a state in which physical and/or mental performance is reduced as a result of these
158	
159	                                                    disturbances.1 Similarly recovery is defined as the set of processes resulting in an athlete’s
160	
161	                                                    renewed ability to meet or exceed previous performance levels, and the recovery period is
162	
163	
164	
165	
166	Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 06/23/19
167	                                                    defined as the time necessary for the various physiological parameters that were altered by
168	
169	                                                    exercise to return to resting values.1
170	
171	                                                             A primary responsibility for scientists and coaches is to understand and manage the
172	
173	                                                    fatigue that athletes encounter in training and competition. To achieve this, a variety of data
174	
175	                                                    regarding the training load and the athlete´s responses to these loads are often used to estimate
176	
177	                                                    the individual state of recovery and/or the need for recovery interventions. However, various
178	
179	                                                    physiological and biochemical systems require different recovery periods, which is important
180	
181	                                                    to consider when scheduling a specific type and timing of recovery interventions (e.g. cold-
182	
183	                                                    water immersion, compression garments or massage). Furthermore, the magnitude of fatigue
184	
185	                                                    in these systems depends on the type/mode, duration and intensity of the previous exercise. It
186	
187	                                                    is noteworthy that available monitoring parameters are usually reflecting only one
188	
189	                                                    physiological aspect of fatigue and recovery, and therefore their time course might deviate from
190	
191	                                                    each other. Therefore, an understanding of the mechanisms driving recovery is important to
192	
193	                                                    estimate if a specific intervention is adequate to enhance performance recovery.
194	
195	                                                             Furthermore, throughout their preparation process athletes periodize their training to
196	
197	                                                    maximize adaptations. This may include specific periods of (intended) insufficient recovery
198	                                                     “The Temporal Relationship Between Exercise, Recovery Processes and Changes in Performance” by Skorski S et al.
199	                                                    International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
200	                                                    © 2019 Human Kinetics, Inc.
201	
202	
203	                                                    and/or periods of (functional) “overload” or “overreaching”.2 These alterations in the training
204	
205	                                                    stimulus highlight the need to adapt recovery time frames and interventions according to the
206	
207	                                                    specific period, the demands of training and the specific needs of the athlete. Failing to meet
208	
209	                                                    an athlete´s recovery needs may lead to an excessive accumulation of fatigue, resulting in
210	
211	                                                    reduced training tolerance and performance, increased risk of illness and injury, as well as
212	
213	                                                    cognitive and mood disturbances.
214	
215	                                                             The aim of this overview is to provide a framework for coaches, athletes and sport
216	
217	                                                    scientists to differentiate physiological load-adaptation pathways (cardiocirculatory,
218	
219	                                                    metabolic, neuromuscular and central) and their different time course of action. Specifically,
220	
221	
222	
223	
224	Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 06/23/19
225	                                                    this review shall provide a physiology-based rationale for an appropriate use of recovery
226	
227	                                                    (interventions) in different training and competition scenarios.
228	
229	                                                    Time-course of physiological recovery
230	
231	                                                             The overall aim of training is to elicit the desired physiological (and other) adaptations
232	
233	                                                    by targeted stimuli.3 A training session generally results in stress and an acute disturbance of
234	
235	                                                    the homeostasis. This triggers adaptations that underpin athletic performance through increased
236	
237	                                                    endurance, speed, strength and/or power. An acute consequence of the physical demand of
238	
239	                                                    training is fatigue, manifesting in negative physiological, functional, and perceptual outcomes,
240	
241	                                                    which can be present up to several days post-exercise. Regardless of the purpose of the ensuing
242	
243	                                                    exercise session (i.e. training or competition), it is crucial to understand the importance of
244	
245	                                                    optimizing the recovery between training bouts, in order to expedite the regenerative processes
246	
247	                                                    and facilitate recovery. After a training session, these acute responses are reverted to (or
248	
249	                                                    beyond) their initial state. However, in the context of physiology, exercise-induced fatigue and
250	
251	                                                    subsequent recovery integrates alterations in many different systems, each following a different
252	
253	                                                    time course, depending on the exercise mode, duration and intensity.4 Specific resistance
254	
255	                                                    training stimulus (e. g. strength-power) fatigues the neuromuscular system specific to strength-
256	                                                     “The Temporal Relationship Between Exercise, Recovery Processes and Changes in Performance” by Skorski S et al.
257	                                                    International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
258	                                                    © 2019 Human Kinetics, Inc.
259	
260	
261	                                                    power stimuli, whereas a specific endurance training (partly) exhausts the aerobic energy
262	
263	                                                    production system. However, it is important to understand that, any exercise training will
264	
265	                                                    challenge both metabolic and neuromuscular systems at different levels depending on its
266	
267	                                                    specific content.5 It seems logical that the type and amount of post-exercise fatigue varies
268	
269	                                                    between the physiological systems, depending on the aforementioned variables. For example,
270	
271	                                                    in endurance sports an increase in external load (e. g. speed, power) leads to an increase in
272	
273	                                                    metabolic cost, requiring augmented provision of fuel substrates and oxygen, challenging the
274	
275	                                                    cardiorespiratory and the metabolic systems.6 In addition to these types of load stimuli, team
276	
277	                                                    sport athletes are also challenged with accelerations and decelerations inducing a mechanical
278	
279	                                                    load component, which needs to be considered when evaluating the need for recovery.7
280	
281	
282	
283	
284	Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 06/23/19
285	                                                             The physical demands of the exercise influence the magnitude of fatigue, the systems
286	
287	                                                    involved and the need for (optimal) recovery. Additionally, fatigue-induced changes seem to
288	
289	                                                    vary within and between individuals.8-10 Hence, the definition of one specific time frame for
290	
291	                                                    post-exercise recovery is difficult as recovery time courses most likely differ within and
292	
293	                                                    between the physiological systems of the human body.8 This implies the need for an
294	
295	                                                    understanding of the fatigue mechanisms that contribute to the performance decrement as well
296	
297	                                                    as their time course to recover.11
298	
299	                                                    Metabolic Recovery
300	
301	                                                             The elevated energy expenditure caused by training and competition reduces substrate
302	
303	                                                    availability, which can decrease performance capacity. In high intensity exercise, any decrease
304

                                                    Abstract

                                                    Physiological and psychological demands during training and competition generate fatigue and

                                                    reduce an athlete´s sport-specific performance capacity. The magnitude of this decrement

                                                    depends on several characteristics of the exercise stimulus (e.g. type, duration, intensity) as

                                                    well as on individual characteristics (e. g. fitness, profile, fatigue resistance). As such, the time

                                                    required to fully recover is proportional to the level of fatigue and the consequences of exercise-

                                                    induced fatigue are manifold. Whatever the purpose of the ensuing exercise session (i.e.

                                                    training or competition), it is crucial to understand the importance of optimizing the period

                                                    between exercise bouts, in order to speed up the regenerative processes and facilitate recovery




Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 06/23/19
                                                    or set the next stimulus at the optimal time point. This implies having a fairly precise

                                                    understanding of the fatigue mechanisms that contribute to the performance decrement. Failing

                                                    to respect an athlete´s recovery needs may lead to an excessive accumulation of fatigue, and

                                                    potentially “non-functional overreaching” or to maladaptive training. Although research in this

                                                    area recently increased, considerations regarding the specific time frames for different

                                                    physiological mechanisms in relation to exercise-induced fatigue are still missing.

                                                    Furthermore, recommendations on the timing and dosing of recovery based on these time

                                                    frames are limited. Therefore, the aim of this article is to describe time courses of recovery in

                                                    relation to the exercise type and on different physiological levels. This summary shall support

                                                    coaches, athletes and scientists in their decision-making process by considering the relationship

                                                    of exercise type, physiology and recovery.
                                                     “The Temporal Relationship Between Exercise, Recovery Processes and Changes in Performance” by Skorski S et al.
                                                    International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
                                                    © 2019 Human Kinetics, Inc.


                                                    Introduction

                                                             Each physical training session provides athletes with physiological stress, leading to

                                                    disturbances in homeostasis of a number of physiological processes and biochemical pathways.

                                                    In response to this stress, the body triggers post-exercise adaptive reactions that counteract

                                                    these physiological and biochemical changes, emphasizing the necessity for an adequate

                                                    recovery period after the training bout. For the purposes of this commentary fatigue is defined

                                                    as a state in which physical and/or mental performance is reduced as a result of these

                                                    disturbances.1 Similarly recovery is defined as the set of processes resulting in an athlete’s

                                                    renewed ability to meet or exceed previous performance levels, and the recovery period is




Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 06/23/19
                                                    defined as the time necessary for the various physiological parameters that were altered by

                                                    exercise to return to resting values.1

                                                             A primary responsibility for scientists and coaches is to understand and manage the

                                                    fatigue that athletes encounter in training and competition. To achieve this, a variety of data

                                                    regarding the training load and the athlete´s responses to these loads are often used to estimate

                                                    the individual state of recovery and/or the need for recovery interventions. However, various

                                                    physiological and biochemical systems require different recovery periods, which is important

                                                    to consider when scheduling a specific type and timing of recovery interventions (e.g. cold-

                                                    water immersion, compression garments or massage). Furthermore, the magnitude of fatigue

                                                    in these systems depends on the type/mode, duration and intensity of the previous exercise. It

                                                    is noteworthy that available monitoring parameters are usually reflecting only one

                                                    physiological aspect of fatigue and recovery, and therefore their time course might deviate from

                                                    each other. Therefore, an understanding of the mechanisms driving recovery is important to

                                                    estimate if a specific intervention is adequate to enhance performance recovery.

                                                             Furthermore, throughout their preparation process athletes periodize their training to

                                                    maximize adaptations. This may include specific periods of (intended) insufficient recovery
                                                     “The Temporal Relationship Between Exercise, Recovery Processes and Changes in Performance” by Skorski S et al.
                                                    International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
                                                    © 2019 Human Kinetics, Inc.


                                                    and/or periods of (functional) “overload” or “overreaching”.2 These alterations in the training

                                                    stimulus highlight the need to adapt recovery time frames and interventions according to the

                                                    specific period, the demands of training and the specific needs of the athlete. Failing to meet

                                                    an athlete´s recovery needs may lead to an excessive accumulation of fatigue, resulting in

                                                    reduced training tolerance and performance, increased risk of illness and injury, as well as

                                                    cognitive and mood disturbances.

                                                             The aim of this overview is to provide a framework for coaches, athletes and sport

                                                    scientists to differentiate physiological load-adaptation pathways (cardiocirculatory,

                                                    metabolic, neuromuscular and central) and their different time course of action. Specifically,




Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 06/23/19
                                                    this review shall provide a physiology-based rationale for an appropriate use of recovery

                                                    (interventions) in different training and competition scenarios.

                                                    Time-course of physiological recovery

                                                             The overall aim of training is to elicit the desired physiological (and other) adaptations

                                                    by targeted stimuli.3 A training session generally results in stress and an acute disturbance of

                                                    the homeostasis. This triggers adaptations that underpin athletic performance through increased

                                                    endurance, speed, strength and/or power. An acute consequence of the physical demand of

                                                    training is fatigue, manifesting in negative physiological, functional, and perceptual outcomes,

                                                    which can be present up to several days post-exercise. Regardless of the purpose of the ensuing

                                                    exercise session (i.e. training or competition), it is crucial to understand the importance of

                                                    optimizing the recovery between training bouts, in order to expedite the regenerative processes

                                                    and facilitate recovery. After a training session, these acute responses are reverted to (or

                                                    beyond) their initial state. However, in the context of physiology, exercise-induced fatigue and

                                                    subsequent recovery integrates alterations in many different systems, each following a different

                                                    time course, depending on the exercise mode, duration and intensity.4 Specific resistance

                                                    training stimulus (e. g. strength-power) fatigues the neuromuscular system specific to strength-
                                                     “The Temporal Relationship Between Exercise, Recovery Processes and Changes in Performance” by Skorski S et al.
                                                    International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
                                                    © 2019 Human Kinetics, Inc.


                                                    power stimuli, whereas a specific endurance training (partly) exhausts the aerobic energy

                                                    production system. However, it is important to understand that, any exercise training will

                                                    challenge both metabolic and neuromuscular systems at different levels depending on its

                                                    specific content.5 It seems logical that the type and amount of post-exercise fatigue varies

                                                    between the physiological systems, depending on the aforementioned variables. For example,

                                                    in endurance sports an increase in external load (e. g. speed, power) leads to an increase in

                                                    metabolic cost, requiring augmented provision of fuel substrates and oxygen, challenging the

                                                    cardiorespiratory and the metabolic systems.6 In addition to these types of load stimuli, team

                                                    sport athletes are also challenged with accelerations and decelerations inducing a mechanical

                                                    load component, which needs to be considered when evaluating the need for recovery.7




Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 06/23/19
                                                             The physical demands of the exercise influence the magnitude of fatigue, the systems

                                                    involved and the need for (optimal) recovery. Additionally, fatigue-induced changes seem to

                                                    vary within and between individuals.8-10 Hence, the definition of one specific time frame for

                                                    post-exercise recovery is difficult as recovery time courses most likely differ within and

                                                    between the physiological systems of the human body.8 This implies the need for an

                                                    understanding of the fatigue mechanisms that contribute to the performance decrement as well

                                                    as their time course to recover.11

                                                    Metabolic Recovery

                                                             The elevated energy expenditure caused by training and competition reduces substrate

                                                    availability, which can decrease performance capacity. In high intensity exercise, any decrease

                                                    in substrate availability has the potential to decrease performance. For example, in brief, high

                                                    intensity exercise, phosphocreatine stores decrease very rapidly reducing the force generating

                                                    capacity.12 However, given the speed of its recovery kinetics,12 phosphocreatine stores may be

                                                    a limiting factor when short recovery periods are available (i.e. the recovery between

                                                    repetitions or sets within the same training session), but it is not considered as a (limiting)
                                                     “The Temporal Relationship Between Exercise, Recovery Processes and Changes in Performance” by Skorski S et al.
                                                    International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
                                                    © 2019 Human Kinetics, Inc.


                                                    factor in recovery for competition or training bouts separated by hours or days. Conversely,

                                                    muscle glycogen resynthesis is much slower and may continue for 2 – 3 days after high

                                                    Neuromuscular Recovery

                                                             Peripheral fatigue refers to decrements in neuromuscular function, e.g. disruptions of

                                                    the potential propagation, excitation-contraction coupling, or cross-bridging cycling, despite

                                                    unchanged or increased neural drive.20 Mechanical disruptions to the muscle fiber are task

                                                    dependent and related to the volume of high intensity contractions (e.g. in particular

                                                    decelerations/accelerations, and/or direction changes).21 The resulting delayed onset muscle

                                                    soreness (DOMS) can be associated with elevated levels of membrane damage markers (e.g.

                                                    creatine kinase, CK) and systematic inflammation indicators like C-reactive protein (CRP).

                                                    This may be accompanied by decreases of both the maximal voluntary contraction force

                                                    (MVC) and the joint range of motion.13 However, the time required to fully recover is related

                                                    to the muscle mass involved and the intensity of the exercise, and ranges from 24 to 96 h.11

                                                    Since the ability of the muscle to generate high levels of forces is involved in many facets of

                                                    athletic performance, the consequences of exercise-induced neuromuscular fatigue are

                                                    manifold.

                                                    Cardiocirculatory Recovery

                                                             A negative fluid balance is common after prolonged and/or intense training sessions.

                                                    The level of dehydration, which depends on environmental conditions (i.e. temperature,

                                                    humidity), can reach up to 4% of body mass.11,13 It is not known whether such a deficit has an

                                                    impact on anaerobic performance,11,13 however, it undoubtedly alters endurance performance.

                                                    In fact, the main consequence of the exercise-induced hypovolemia is a decrease in stroke

                                                    volume, and a tightly coupled increase in heart rate to maintain cardiac output. This alteration

                                                    in turn decreases maximal oxygen uptake (due to the reduced remaining capacity to increase

                                                    heart rate) and related fitness components such as repeated sprint ability, but also the capacity

                                                    to maintain core temperature, which is considered as an important determinant for the

                                                    perception of fatigue.34 The time required to return to euhydration is difficult to establish, since

                                                    it depends on a number of factors including the level of post-exercise dehydration, the volume

                                                    of ingested fluid, its temperature and the composition as well as the speed of gastric emptying.

                                                    However, it can be relatively short (6 h) provided all recommendations are fulfilled.35

                                                    Performance Recovery

                                                             Irrespective of the physiological underpinnings of recovery, it is clearly more critical

                                                    for coaches and athletes to understand its impact on physical performance. In team sport

                                                    athletes maximal strength,18,23 vertical jump ability23,30 and sprint performance18,22,23 are

                                                    significantly impaired immediately post-exercise with a time to fully recover of 12 to > 72 h.

                                                    The duration and magnitude of the performance decrement vary between studies, as these

                                                    effects obviously depend on the exercise type as well as intensity and individual

                                                    characteristics.23 For example, in endurance athletes Skorski et al.39 did not observe a

                                                    meaningful reduction in cycling performance (40-km time trial) after a 6-d intensive training

                                                    camp in 10 out of the 23 cyclists involved. Even though it has been stated that the assessment

                                                    of a decrement in sports-specific performance represents the gold standard for measuring short-

                                                    term fatigue in athletes, it might be speculated that fatigue-related performance decrements

                                                    may be maintained despite measurable physiological changes.

                                                    Planning recovery in training and competition

                                                             Because insufficient recovery prevents athletes from training/competing at the required

                                                    intensity or completing the required load in the upcoming training session, often active

                                                    recovery interventions are undertaken after training and competition to enhance the recovery

                                                    process. Such interventions are reported to shift the stress-recovery balance towards recovery.

                                                    Thus, strategies that minimize fatigue and/or accelerate recovery after training are considered

                                                    beneficial, as they can facilitate an athlete’s readiness for further training or competition.

                                                    Conclusion

                                                             The effects of fatigue and recovery on performance in training and competition are

                                                    complex. The fatigue resultant from a training session depends on the specific training stimulus

                                                    and the extent of the stress in the various physiological systems. These systems can require

                                                    different recovery periods for complete restoration of homeostasis. Additionally, despite a vast

                                                    amount of research evaluating the efficacy of various recovery interventions a ´one-size-fits-

                                                    all´ approach does not appear to be appropriate. Indeed, recovery strategies should be tailored

                                                    to the need of the individual athlete and carefully periodizied throughout a season, given that

                                                    too much recovery and/or specific interventions might blunt training adaptation. Further

                                                    research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness of recovery interventions based on the type of

   "abstract":"A brief review of the time courses of recovery across physiological systems after training and competition, and how they relate to changes in performance. The authors argue that recovery should be tailored to the individual athlete and periodized across the season.",
   "tldr":"Different physiological systems recover on different timelines, and those timelines rarely match the return of performance. Recovery strategies should be individualized and periodized, because too much recovery can blunt training adaptation.",

   "findings":"In team-sport athletes, maximal strength, vertical jump and sprint performance are significantly impaired immediately after exercise, with full recovery taking 12 to more than 72 h. Inflammation markers peak 24 to 48 h after a soccer match and return to baseline by 48 to 120 h, while neuromuscular function returns to baseline between 5 and 96 h.    "limitations":"No systematic search is described, and the authors do not state how studies were selected.    "practicalImplications":"Staff should plan recovery around the training stimulus, since different systems recover on different timelines, rather than applying one fixed recovery window.    "athleteDev":"Use the different recovery timelines to space hard sessions, and track neuromuscular and performance measures across days rather than relying on one marker. Match recovery interventions to the training phase, since the authors note that regular cold water immersion has been linked to blunted strength-training adaptation in some studies.",
   "rtp":"The review supports using jump and sprint measures to judge recovery from team-sport exercise, since those return to baseline over roughly 5 to 96 h.     RESEARCH ARTICLE                    OPEN ACCESS




The Thiol Oxidation State of Albumin Is Associated With
Training Load Across an Australian Football Pre-Season
Christopher James1            | Jason Weber2,3            | Corrin Boyde4           | Paul A. Fournier5            | Peter G. Arthur1
1
 School of Molecular Sciences, The University of Western Australia, Perth, Western Australia, Australia | 2UWA Tech and Policy Lab, The University of Western
Australia, Perth, Western Australia, Australia | 3SpeedSig, Perth, Western Australia, Australia | 4School of Veterinary Medicine, Murdoch University, Murdoch,
Western Australia, Australia | 5School of Human Sciences, Department of Sport Science, Exercise and Health, The University of Western Australia, Perth,
Western Australia, Australia

Correspondence: Peter G. Arthur (peter.arthur@uwa.edu.au)

Received: 19 January 2025 | Revised: 5 January 2026 | Accepted: 13 February 2026

Academic Editor: Amjad Islam Aqib

Keywords: Australian football | COVID-19 | dried blood spot | exercise-induced muscle damage | oxidative stress | OxiDx | thiol-oxidised albumin | training load


    ABSTRACT
    Australian football is a demanding contact sport where high training loads during the pre-season have been identiﬁed as a
    potential cause of non-contact injuries. The level of thiol-oxidised albumin, a marker of oxidative stress, might be related to the
    training load, and thus could be used to indirectly quantify the impact of training loads upon an athlete. The aim of this study was
    to investigate whether the level of thiol-oxidised albumin was affected by the pre-season training load in a team of professional
    Australian Football League (AFL) athletes and compare the effect of lower pre-season training loads caused by COVID-19
    restrictions on the level of thiol-oxidised albumin. Forty-ﬁve participants collected daily dried blood spots in the morning prior
    to each training session to measure thiol-oxidised albumin using a novel methodology (OxiDx). Training load, which was
    operationally deﬁned as the total distance covered during training as well as distance at certain velocities, and change of direction
    (COD), was measured using global positioning units. There was an association (R2 = 0.12) between the level of thiol-oxidised
    albumin with; (1) total distance covered (p <0:0001), (2) distance covered at 10–20 km/h (p <0:0001) and 20–25 km/h (p ¼ 0:0082)
    and (3) COD running (p ¼ 0:0025). Training loads and the level of thiol-oxidised albumin were highest in the early pre-season and
    lowest at the conclusion of the pre-season, when training loads were reduced as a consequence of COVID-19. The measurement of
    the level of thiol-oxidised albumin may provide a means to indirectly quantify the impact of training loads upon an athlete,
    especially given the simplicity of the OxiDx methodology for ﬁngertip blood sample collection.

 CURRENT OPINION



The Trade Secret Taboo: Open Science Methods are Required
to Improve Prediction Models in Sports Medicine and Performance
Garrett S. Bullock1,2,3 · Patrick Ward4 · Franco M. Impellizzeri5 · Stefan Kluzek3,6,7 · Tom Hughes8,9 ·
Paula Dhiman10,11 · Richard D. Riley12 · Gary S. Collins10,11

Accepted: 25 March 2023
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023


Abstract
Clinical prediction models in sports medicine that utilize regression or machine learning techniques have become more
widely published, used, and disseminated. However, these models are typically characterized by poor methodology and
incomplete reporting, and an inadequate evaluation of performance, leading to unreliable predictions and weak clinical util-
ity within their intended sport population. Before implementation in practice, models require a thorough evaluation. Strong
replicable methods and transparency reporting allow practitioners and researchers to make independent judgments as to the
model’s validity, performance, clinical usefulness, and confidence it will do no harm. However, this is not reflected in the
sports medicine literature. As shown in a recent systematic review of models for predicting sports injury models, most were
typically characterized by poor methodology, incomplete reporting, and inadequate performance evaluation. Because of
constraints imposed by data from individual teams, the development of accurate, reliable, and useful models is highly reliant
on external validation. However, a barrier to collaboration is a desire to maintain a competitive advantage; a team’s propri-
etary information is often perceived as high value, and so these ‘trade secrets’ are frequently guarded. These ‘trade secrets’
also apply to commercially available models, as developers are unwilling to share proprietary (and potentially profitable)
development and validation information. In this Current Opinion, we: (1) argue that open science is essential for improving
sport prediction models and (2) critically examine sport prediction models for open science practices.

 "decision":"INCLUDE",

 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The title in the text, The Trade Secret Taboo: Open Science Methods are Required to Improve Prediction Models in Sports Medicine and Performance, matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Monitoring & Technology"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Research & Analytics","Performance"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"A Current Opinion arguing that open science (shared data, code, protocols and transparent reporting) is needed to improve sports prediction models. The authors extracted open-science practices from the 30 studies in an earlier systematic review of sports injury prediction models, and found that only one (3%) had a public protocol, three (10%) reported TRIPOD adherence, and none shared model code or data.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The 30-study extraction comes from a single earlier review, so it describes that set of studies rather than the whole sports literature. The recommendations are opinion-based and were not tested in a study.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the conclusion that no published sport prediction model is viable as a general verdict, when it rests on the reporting and validation of one earlier set of 30 injury prediction studies.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2023,
   "citation":"Bullock GS, Ward P, Impellizzeri FM, et al. The Trade Secret Taboo: Open Science Methods are Required to Improve Prediction Models in Sports Medicine and Performance. Sports Medicine. 2023.",
   "doi":"10.1007/s40279-023-01849-6",
   "abstract":"Argues that sports prediction models are poorly developed and reported, partly because teams guard their data as trade secrets. Using open-science data from a prior systematic review of 30 sports injury prediction studies, the authors show that sharing practices were almost absent and call for shared data, code and protocols.",
   "tldr":"Sports prediction models are rarely built or validated in ways others can check, and team data is often kept private. Sharing de-identified data, code and protocols would allow larger and more reliable models.",
   "methods":"Current Opinion with a secondary extraction of open-science practices from the 30 studies in an earlier systematic review of sports injury prediction models. Practices assessed were protocol availability, study registration, TRIPOD reporting, data sharing, and availability of the model equation or code. The paper also describes options such as gatekeeper data warehouses and synthetic data sets.",
   "findings":"Only one of the 30 studies (3%) made its protocol publicly available, and that same study was the only one registered. Three (10%) reported following TRIPOD, four (13%) reported the full model equation, and no machine learning study provided model code. No study deposited data in an open-access database or shared it, although four used open-access datasets available online.",
   "limitations":"The extraction covers one earlier set of 30 studies, so it does not measure the wider sports literature. The paper is an opinion piece with recommendations that were not tested, and the authors acknowledge that journal incentives and limited open-science training also contribute to poor practice.",
   "practicalImplications":"Before using an injury-risk or load model, staff should ask whether it was validated on other squads and whether its method, code and data are available to check. Clubs could share de-identified data through gatekeeper warehouses or synthetic data sets to build larger samples without revealing athlete identity.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: A training-load or readiness model is only as trustworthy as its validation, so staff should check that any model was tested on data outside the squad that built it before relying on it. The paper gives no training prescription or evidence of performance effects.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: The paper concerns injury prediction models in general, not return-to-play decisions. It supports caution about using an unvalidated model to judge an injured athlete's readiness, but it does not evaluate any return-to-play test or criterion."
 }
}

    CURRENT OPINION



The Translation of Sport Science Research to the Field: A Current
Opinion and Overview on the Perceptions of Practitioners, Researchers
and Coaches
Hugh H. K. Fullagar1        · Alan McCall2 · Franco M. Impellizzeri1 · Terry Favero3 · Aaron J. Coutts1


© Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2019


Abstract
Evidence-based practice (EBP) is the collated integration of practitioner expertise, athlete values and research evidence aimed
to optimise the decision-making process surrounding sport performance. Despite the academic interest afforded to sport sci-
ence research, our knowledge of how this research is applied in elite sport settings is limited. This current opinion examines
the existing evidence of the translation of sport science research into the field, with a tailored focus on the current perceptions
of practitioners, researchers and coaches. Recent studies show that practitioners and researchers report they ascertain sport
science knowledge differently, with coaches preferring personal interactions compared with coaching courses or scientific
journals. The limited peer-reviewed research shows that coaches perceive their knowledge is greater in fields such as tactical/
technical areas, rather than physical fitness or general conditioning. This likely explains coaches’ greater perceived value
in research dedicated to technical and tactical expertise, as well as mental training and skill acquisition. Practitioners place
a large emphasis on the need for research in physical fitness areas, which is likely due to their occupational focus. There
are many perceived barriers of sport science research application, including funding, time, coach/player/staff ‘buy in’ and
research questions that may not apply to the setting. We contend that researchers and practitioners may benefit in producing
research, ascertaining knowledge and disseminating findings in alternative methods that better align with coaches’ needs. In
addition, educational strategies that focus on real-world context and promote social interaction between coaches, practition-
ers, organisational personnel and researchers would likely benefit all stakeholders.

Coaches value research on mental training, tactics and technical efficiency most, while practitioners and researchers value fitness and recovery research and rate research embedded in clubs as most applicable. Reported barriers include funding and time for practitioners, staff and manager buy-in for researchers, and research questions that do not match coaches' needs.",
   "limitations":"The paper describes itself as an opinion piece and reports no search method, so the evidence base cannot be audited.    "athleteDev":"Performance Application: Introduce new monitoring or analysis only after agreeing a shared performance goal and each person's role with the coach. 5	Absorptiometry (DEXA) in Evaluating
6	Recovery After Musculoskeletal
7	Injuries in Athletes
8	A Scoping Review
9	Robert DiCesare,* MD, MSc, Umair Tahir,y MD(c), Atefeh Noori,z PhD, Norah F. Matthies,*§ MD,
10	FRCSC, Jaskarndip Chahal,*§ MD, FRCSC, Ryan A. Paul,*zz MD, FRCSC,
11	and Andrea H.W. Chan,*||{ MD, FRCSC
12	Investigation performed at University of Toronto, Division of Orthopaedic Surgery,
13	Toronto, Ontario, Canada
14	
15	Background: Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) is a widely used imaging modality in sports medicine and orthopaedics
16	due to its accuracy in assessing bone mineral density (BMD) and body composition. Tracking these parameters provides valuable
17	insights into the recovery process after musculoskeletal injuries, which are prevalent among athletes.
18	Purpose: To evaluate how DEXA imaging has been used to guide rehabilitation in both recreational and competitive athletes by
19	monitoring changes in BMD and body composition after musculoskeletal injuries.
20	Study Design: Scoping review; Level of evidence, 4.
21	Methods: A comprehensive literature search was conducted in Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Central, and SportDISCUS
22	databases (2000-2024). Studies were included if they used DEXA to measure BMD or body composition changes in athletes after
23	musculoskeletal injuries. Titles, abstracts, and full texts were screened independently by 2 reviewers, with discrepancies resolved
24	through discussion. Data were synthesized qualitatively, and major trends were reported and identified.
25	Results: Of 1132 unique records, 12 studies met inclusion criteria, involving 319 athletes (34% female) with injuries such as ante-
26	rior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears, lumbar stress fractures, femoroacetabular impingement, and Achilles tendon ruptures. Athletes
27	represented a range of sports, including soccer, basketball, cricket, and triathlon, at both competitive and recreational levels.
28	DEXA identified significant BMD declines after injury, particularly in the affected limb. For instance, up to a 7% BMD reduction
29	was observed in surgical limbs after ACL reconstruction, persisting for up to 2 years in some cases. Rehabilitation strategies
30	incorporating blood flow restriction therapy or combined running and isometric exercises better preserved lean mass and
31	BMD compared with conventional programs focused solely on closed and open kinetic chain exercises.
32	Conclusion: The review demonstrated that DEXA imaging is a promising tool in orthopaedic sports medicine for assessing injury-
33	related changes in BMD and body composition. It provides detailed insights into recovery processes and aids in tailoring reha-
34	bilitation strategies and return-to-sport decisions. Some studies incorporated advanced rehabilitation methods such as blood
35	flow restriction therapy, which appeared to accelerate recovery as measured by DEXA outcomes. Future studies should explore
36	integrating DEXA findings into athlete-specific rehabilitation protocols with validated thresholds for return to play.
37	Keywords: dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry; DEXA; body composition; rehabilitation; return-to-play
