Review


The Use of Dual-Energy X-ray
Absorptiometry (DEXA) in Evaluating
Recovery After Musculoskeletal
Injuries in Athletes
A Scoping Review
Robert DiCesare,* MD, MSc, Umair Tahir,y MD(c), Atefeh Noori,z PhD, Norah F. Matthies,*§ MD,
FRCSC, Jaskarndip Chahal,*§ MD, FRCSC, Ryan A. Paul,*zz MD, FRCSC,
and Andrea H.W. Chan,*||{ MD, FRCSC
Investigation performed at University of Toronto, Division of Orthopaedic Surgery,
Toronto, Ontario, Canada

Background: Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) is a widely used imaging modality in sports medicine and orthopaedics
due to its accuracy in assessing bone mineral density (BMD) and body composition. Tracking these parameters provides valuable
insights into the recovery process after musculoskeletal injuries, which are prevalent among athletes.
Purpose: To evaluate how DEXA imaging has been used to guide rehabilitation in both recreational and competitive athletes by
monitoring changes in BMD and body composition after musculoskeletal injuries.
Study Design: Scoping review; Level of evidence, 4.
Methods: A comprehensive literature search was conducted in Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Central, and SportDISCUS
databases (2000-2024). Studies were included if they used DEXA to measure BMD or body composition changes in athletes after
musculoskeletal injuries. Titles, abstracts, and full texts were screened independently by 2 reviewers, with discrepancies resolved
through discussion. Data were synthesized qualitatively, and major trends were reported and identified.
Results: Of 1132 unique records, 12 studies met inclusion criteria, involving 319 athletes (34% female) with injuries such as ante-
rior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears, lumbar stress fractures, femoroacetabular impingement, and Achilles tendon ruptures. Athletes
represented a range of sports, including soccer, basketball, cricket, and triathlon, at both competitive and recreational levels.
DEXA identified significant BMD declines after injury, particularly in the affected limb. For instance, up to a 7% BMD reduction
was observed in surgical limbs after ACL reconstruction, persisting for up to 2 years in some cases. Rehabilitation strategies
incorporating blood flow restriction therapy or combined running and isometric exercises better preserved lean mass and
BMD compared with conventional programs focused solely on closed and open kinetic chain exercises.
Conclusion: The review demonstrated that DEXA imaging is a promising tool in orthopaedic sports medicine for assessing injury-
related changes in BMD and body composition. It provides detailed insights into recovery processes and aids in tailoring reha-
bilitation strategies and return-to-sport decisions. Some studies incorporated advanced rehabilitation methods such as blood
flow restriction therapy, which appeared to accelerate recovery as measured by DEXA outcomes. Future studies should explore
integrating DEXA findings into athlete-specific rehabilitation protocols with validated thresholds for return to play.
Keywords: dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry; DEXA; body composition; rehabilitation; return-to-play

 "evidenceSummary":"A PRISMA-ScR scoping review of 12 studies with 319 athletes (34% female), mostly after anterior cruciate ligament injury or reconstruction, that used DEXA to track bone mineral density and lean mass during recovery. Bone density typically fell about 4-10% in the first 6 months after injury or surgery and recovered over 12-25 months in ACL studies, and the only randomised trial found that blood flow restriction therapy preserved more lean mass and bone and shortened time to return to sport (6.42 vs 8.30 months).",
 "screeningLimitations":"Most included studies were observational or single-case reports with small samples, only one was a randomised trial, and no formal risk-of-bias assessment was done. The evidence is dominated by ACL studies with few upper-body injuries, and scanning protocols varied.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat DEXA bone and lean-mass changes as validated return-to-play markers, when the authors state that validated return-to-play thresholds are still needed.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2025,
   "citation":"DiCesare R, Tahir U, Noori A, et al. The Use of Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DEXA) in Evaluating Recovery After Musculoskeletal Injuries in Athletes: A Scoping Review. The Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025;13(11):23259671251387342.",
   "doi":"10.1177/23259671251387342",
   "abstract":"A scoping review of 12 studies (319 athletes, 34% female) on how DEXA has been used to track bone mineral density and body composition during recovery from musculoskeletal injury. Bone density fell after injury, mostly in the injured limb, and some rehabilitation approaches preserved bone and lean mass better than others.",
   "tldr":"DEXA can track bone and lean-mass loss after musculoskeletal injury in athletes. Bone density often fell 4-10% in the first 6 months and recovered over 12-25 months after ACL injury, but the evidence is small and mostly observational, so DEXA is a monitoring tool rather than a return-to-play test.",
   "methods":"PRISMA-ScR scoping review of Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane CENTRAL and SportDISCUS (2000-2024) with two reviewers screening independently. Included studies had athletes with musculoskeletal injury, a baseline DEXA scan near the injury site and at least one follow-up scan. Because designs were heterogeneous, the results were synthesised narratively.",
   "findings":"Of 1132 unique records, 12 studies were included, seven of them on ACL reconstruction. Bone mineral density typically fell about 4-10% in the first 6 months after injury or surgery and was near baseline by 24 months in several ACL studies, and injured limbs lost about 7-14% lean mass during immobilisation before partial to full recovery. In the one randomised trial (17 athletes with blood flow restriction, 15 controls), time to return to sport was shorter with blood flow restriction (6.42 vs 8.30 months), and that group kept lean mass and lost less bone.",
   "limitations":"Most studies were observational or single-case reports with small samples, and the authors did not run a formal risk-of-bias assessment. The abstract says that running plus isometric exercise better preserved bone density than conventional programs, but the body reports no conventional comparison for that protocol, so that claim is not supported in the text. The authors also note that DEXA can overestimate trunk lean mass compared with MRI.",
   "practicalImplications":"Serial DEXA scans can show whether an injured limb is losing or regaining bone and lean mass, which can guide loading and rehabilitation intensity. Blood flow restriction is worth discussing when faster return and better lean-mass retention matter, but that rests on one small trial.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: Baseline and serial DEXA scans can track limb asymmetry in lean mass, which the authors link to injury risk above about 10%. The review measures no performance outcomes, so it does not show that DEXA-guided programming improves performance.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: DEXA-measured bone and lean-mass recovery can be read alongside strength and functional tests when planning return to sport after ACL reconstruction or stress injury. The review cannot set return-to-play thresholds, because the authors state that validated thresholds are still needed and most evidence is observational."
 }
}
